title: Why the Romans Feared Their Own Generals
standfirst: A republic that won wars kept creating men too powerful to control.
body: The Roman Republic was designed to stop any one man from ruling. Power was split between two consuls who served for a single year, and the Senate guarded tradition with jealous care. Yet the Republic ended with a general marching on Rome. How did a system so wary of kings produce one?
## Armies that belonged to their commanders

In the early Republic, soldiers were citizen farmers who served for a campaign and went home. As Rome expanded, wars grew longer and further away. The reforms associated with Gaius Marius opened the legions to men without property, who looked to their general for pay, land and a future.

The result was a new kind of loyalty. Soldiers owed their prospects not to the state but to the man who led them. A popular general now had something no consul had held before: a private army in all but name.

Every great conquest made the problem worse. Victory brought plunder, glory and a devoted following. Sulla showed what that could mean when he turned his legions on Rome itself in 88 BC. Once it had been done, it could be done again.

Pompey and Caesar each rose on the back of foreign wars. The Senate tried to balance one against the other, and in doing so made both more dangerous. When Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC, he was following a path that others had already cleared.

Augustus, who ended the civil wars, understood the danger better than anyone. He made himself the paymaster of every legion and kept the frontier armies under men he trusted. The Republic had feared its generals with good reason. The empire solved the problem by making one general permanent.
